# Overview



DIMOS (Differentiable Molecular Simulator) is a PyTorch-based framework designed for molecular dynamics (MD) and Monte Carlo (MC) simulations that bridges the gap between traditional simulation engines and modern machine learning workflows. The framework is built for flexibility, performance, and end-to-end differentiability, enabling seamless integration with contemporary ML pipelines for scientific computing. DIMOS supports both classical force fields and modern machine learning potentials, making it suitable for a wide range of computational chemistry and materials science applications.

![DIMOS Logo](https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS/blob/public-branch/dimos-logo.svg?raw=true)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L15)

## What Makes DIMOS Different

DIMOS distinguishes itself through its differentiable architecture and PyTorch foundation. Unlike traditional molecular simulation packages that operate as black boxes, DIMOS exposes every computation through PyTorch's automatic differentiation system. This design choice enables gradient-based optimization of simulation parameters, end-to-end training of neural network potentials, and innovative hybrid approaches that combine classical molecular mechanics with machine learning methods. The framework leverages PyTorch's GPU acceleration capabilities to achieve competitive performance while maintaining the flexibility to implement custom force fields and sampling methods.

The framework supports multiple integrators, thermostats, barostats, and enhanced sampling techniques through a modular architecture. Users can seamlessly switch between different simulation ensembles (NVE, NVT, NPT), choose from various nonbonded interaction methods (cutoff, Ewald, PME), and even combine classical force fields with machine learning potentials for hybrid simulations. This modularity makes DIMOS ideal for research applications requiring methodological flexibility.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L1-L55), [simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L374-L395)

## System Architecture

DIMOS follows a layered architectural design that separates concerns clearly while enabling efficient data flow between components. The system is organized around core modules that handle distinct aspects of molecular simulations:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "User Interface"
        A[Simulation Setup] --> B[Force Field Definition]
        A --> C[Integrator Selection]
        A --> D[Barostat/Thermostat]
    end
    
    subgraph "Core Simulation Engine"
        E[MDSimulation/MCSimulation] --> F[Energy Calculation]
        E --> G[Integrator Integration]
        E --> H[State Management]
    end
    
    subgraph "Energy Framework"
        F --> I[Nonbonded Interactions]
        F --> J[Bonded Interactions]
        F --> K[ML Potentials]
    end
    
    subgraph "Physics Components"
        I --> L[Lennard-Jones]
        I --> M[Electrostatics]
        I --> N[Ewald/PME]
        J --> O[Bonds]
        J --> P[Angles]
        J --> Q[Torsions]
        K --> R[MACE]
        K --> S[ORB]
    end
    
    subgraph "System Control"
        G --> T[Velocity Verlet]
        G --> U[Langevin Dynamics]
        G --> V[Nose-Hoover Chains]
        H --> W[Neighbor Lists]
        H --> X[Periodic Boundaries]
        H --> Y[Constraint Handling]
    end
    
    subgraph "Enhanced Sampling"
        D --> Z[Monte Carlo Barostats]
        A --> AA[Metadynamics]
        A --> AB[Replica Exchange]
    end
    
    style A fill:#e1f5ff
    style E fill:#fff4e1
    style F fill:#e8f5e9
    style K fill:#f3e5f5
```

This architecture enables developers to mix and match components according to their needs. For example, you can combine a classical AMBER force field with a machine learning potential using the MLMMsystem, or switch between Langevin dynamics and Nose-Hoover chains while keeping everything else constant. The differentiable nature of PyTorch tensors propagates through all components, enabling gradient computation through entire simulation workflows.

Sources: [simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L403-L858), [energy.py](/dimos/energy.py#L374-L384), [ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L374-L386)

## Project Structure

The DIMOS repository is organized to support modular development while providing clear separation between core functionality, examples, benchmarks, and tests:

```
dimos/
├── dimos/                  # Core simulation framework
│   ├── advanced_methods/   # Enhanced sampling techniques
│   ├── mlip/              # Machine learning potential interfaces
│   ├── simulation.py      # MD/MC simulation orchestration
│   ├── energy.py          # Energy calculation framework
│   ├── ff.py              # Force field implementations
│   ├── integrators.py     # Time integration methods
│   ├── barostats.py       # Pressure control
│   └── neighbor_handling.py # Neighbor list algorithms
├── examples/              # Example input files
├── benchmark/             # Performance benchmarks
├── experiments/           # Research experiments
└── tests/                 # Test suites
```

The core `dimos/` directory contains the complete simulation framework, with each module handling a specific aspect of molecular simulation. The `advanced_methods/` subdirectory provides implementations of enhanced sampling techniques like metadynamics and replica exchange molecular dynamics. The `mlip/` subdirectory contains interfaces to machine learning interatomic potentials, specifically MACE and ORB models.

Sources: [Repository Structure](/), [advanced_methods/metadynamics.py](/dimos/advanced_methods/metadynamics.py#L374-L393), [mlip/mace.py](/dimos/mlip/mace.py#L374-L387)

## Core Capabilities

DIMOS provides a comprehensive set of capabilities for molecular simulations through its modular components:

### Force Field Support

The framework supports multiple force field formats through unified interfaces:

| Force Field Type | Format | Class | Key Features |
|------------------|--------|-------|--------------|
| AMBER | prmtop/rst7 | `AmberForceField` | Standard AMBER force fields, periodic boundary conditions, multiple nonbonded methods |
| GROMACS | gro/top | `GromacsForceField` | GROMACS topology support, CHARMM-style dihedrals |
| Machine Learning | Pre-trained models | `MaceFoundationalSystem`, `OrbFoundationalSystem` | MACE and ORB potentials, periodic support, CuEq acceleration |
| Hybrid ML/MM | Combination | `MLMMsystem` | ML regions + MM regions, configurable electrostatic coupling |

This support enables users to leverage existing force field parameters while also exploring modern machine learning potentials. The hybrid ML/MM system allows treating specific atoms or regions with ML potentials while using classical force fields for the rest of the system, balancing accuracy and computational efficiency.

Sources: [ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L374-L386), [mlmm.py](/dimos/mlmm.py#L374-L390), [mlip/mace.py](/dimos/mlip/mace.py#L374-L387)

### Integration Methods

DIMOS provides a comprehensive suite of integrators for different simulation scenarios:

| Integrator | Ensemble | Thermostat | Key Use Case |
|------------|----------|------------|--------------|
| Velocity Verlet | NVE | None | Energy conservation testing, microcanonical dynamics |
| Langevin Dynamics | NVT | Langevin | Canonical ensemble, biomolecular simulations |
| Brownian Dynamics | NVT | Friction/Noise | Overdamped dynamics, implicit solvent |
| Andersen Dynamics | NVT | Stochastic collisions | Alternative canonical thermostat |
| Berendsen Dynamics | NVT | Weak coupling | Temperature relaxation (production) |
| Lowe-Andersen | NVT | Stochastic collisions | Improved canonical thermostat |
| Nose-Hoover | NVT | Deterministic | Extended system thermostat |
| Nose-Hoover Chain | NVT | Multiple thermostats | High-performance canonical sampling |

The integrators all inherit from `CommonIntegrator`, ensuring consistent interfaces for timestep management, acceleration updates, and computation graph handling. This design makes it straightforward to switch between different thermostats without changing other simulation components.

Sources: [integrators.py](/dimos/integrators.py#L374-L381)

### Nonbonded Interactions

DIMOS implements multiple methods for computing nonbonded interactions with different trade-offs between accuracy and computational cost:

| Method | Description | Periodic | Cutoff | Best For |
|--------|-------------|----------|--------|----------|
| `NonbondedInteractionsNoCutoff` | Full pair-wise calculation | Yes | No | Small systems, validation |
| `NonbondedInteractionsCutoff` | Truncated with switching function | Yes | Yes | General-purpose simulations |
| `NonbondedInteractionsEwald` | Ewald summation | Yes | Yes | Charged systems without PME |
| `NonbondedInteractionsPME` | Particle Mesh Ewald | Yes | Yes | Large periodic charged systems |

Each method supports Lennard-Jones and electrostatic contributions, with configurable cutoff distances, switching functions, and exclusion handling for bonded atoms. The implementations leverage PyTorch's vectorized operations for efficient computation on CPU and GPU.

Sources: [energy.py](/dimos/energy.py#L402-L932)

## Key Features

### End-to-End Differentiability

Every calculation in DIMOS flows through PyTorch's automatic differentiation system, enabling gradient computation through entire simulation workflows. This differentiability supports several advanced use cases: parameter optimization for force fields, training neural network potentials, and gradient-based sampling methods like Hamiltonian Monte Carlo. The framework provides `detach_()` methods to selectively disconnect tensors from the computation graph, balancing memory efficiency with gradient requirements.

Sources: [simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L668-L676), [simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L845-L852)

### GPU Acceleration

DIMOS leverages PyTorch's native GPU support for accelerated computation. The framework uses vectorized operations optimized for both CPU and GPU execution, with PyTorch's `torch.compile` feature available for additional performance gains. Benchmarks demonstrate competitive performance against traditional simulation engines like OpenMM, especially for larger systems.

Sources: [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](/benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L66-L72)

### Neighbor List Management

Efficient neighbor list algorithms are crucial for scaling simulations to large system sizes. DIMOS implements cell list algorithms with Verlet neighbor lists, supporting both periodic and non-periodic boundary conditions. The system automatically updates neighbor lists based on atomic displacements, with configurable skin distances to balance between update frequency and computational overhead.

Sources: [neighbor_handling.py](/dimos/neighbor_handling.py#L374-L388)

### Enhanced Sampling

The framework includes advanced sampling methods for exploring complex energy landscapes:

- **Metadynamics**: History-dependent bias potentials along collective variables to help systems escape local minima, with well-tempered metadynamics for controlled bias growth
- **Replica Exchange**: Multiple replicas at different temperatures enabling crossing of high energy barriers
- **Monte Carlo Barostats**: Isotropic and anisotropic pressure control for constant pressure simulations

These methods integrate seamlessly with the simulation infrastructure, enabling users to apply them to any force field or potential implementation.

Sources: [advanced_methods/metadynamics.py](/dimos/advanced_methods/metadynamics.py#L374-L393), [barostats.py](/dimos/barostats.py#L374-L385)

## Installation and Dependencies

DIMOS requires Python 3.10 or higher and can be installed via pip or from source. The core dependencies include PyTorch (≥2.4.1), ParmEd (≥4.2.2), and NumPy (<2.0.0). Optional dependencies provide extended functionality:

| Optional Group | Packages | Purpose |
|----------------|----------|---------|
| `dev` | OpenMM, Sphinx, matplotlib | Development and documentation |
| `mmtools` | openmmtools, mdtraj, pymbar | Enhanced sampling and analysis |
| `mace` | mace-torch, cuequivariance-ops-torch-cu12 | MACE ML potentials |
| `orb` | orb-models, pynanoflann | ORB ML potentials |

The modular dependency structure allows users to install only the components they need, keeping the installation footprint minimal for basic use cases while providing access to advanced features when required.

Sources: [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L60), [README.md](/README.md#L17-L30)

## Getting Started Guide

The typical workflow for running a DIMOS simulation involves three main steps: defining the force field system, creating an integrator, and setting up the simulation. Here's a minimal example that demonstrates this pattern:

```python
import dimos

# 1. Define force field system from AMBER topology
system = dimos.AmberForceField("config.prmtop", 
                               cutoff=9, 
                               switch_distance=7.5,
                               nonbonded_type="PME",
                               periodic=True)

# 2. Create integrator with timestep 0.5 fs, temperature 300 K, friction 1.0 ps⁻¹
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(dt=0.5, T=300, gamma=1.0, system=system)

# 3. Initialize simulation with starting positions
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(system, integrator, positions, T=300)

# 4. Run simulation for specified number of steps
simulation.step(num_steps=10000)
```

This example uses the AMBER force field format with PME electrostatics and Langevin dynamics for temperature control. The simulation automatically handles neighbor list updates, periodic boundary conditions, and energy calculations. For different requirements, you can substitute different force fields (e.g., `GromacsForceField`, `MaceFoundationalSystem`), integrators (e.g., `VelocityVerlet`, `NoseHooverChainDynamics`), or add barostats for pressure control.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L33-L42)

# Quick Start



This guide provides beginner-level developers with a fast path to running their first molecular dynamics simulation using DIMOS. You'll learn the essential workflow for setting up and executing simulations, understand the core architecture, and discover where to go next for deeper knowledge.

DIMOS (Differentiable Molecular Simulator) is a PyTorch-based framework that bridges traditional molecular dynamics simulations with modern machine learning workflows. Its modular design enables seamless integration with ML potentials like MACE and ORB while maintaining compatibility with classical force fields from Amber and Gromacs.

![DIMOS Logo](https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS/blob/public-branch/dimos-logo.svg?raw=true)

## Installation

DIMOS can be installed using pip for the core functionality or via git clone for development work with optional dependencies. Choose the installation method that matches your needs.

### Basic Installation

For quick prototyping with Amber/Gromacs force fields:

```bash
pip install dimos-torch
```

This installs the core dependencies: PyTorch (≥2.4.1), ParmEd (≥4.2.2), and NumPy (<2.0.0) [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L39-L44).

### Development Installation

For full functionality including ML potentials and testing tools:

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nec-research/dimos.git; cd dimos

# Install with optional dependencies
python -m pip install -e '.[dev,mmtools,mace,orb]'
```

The optional dependency groups provide:
- **dev**: OpenMM with CUDA, Sphinx documentation tools, matplotlib [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L48-L53)
- **mmtools**: OpenMM tools, MDTraj, PyMBAR for enhanced sampling and analysis [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L55-L61)
- **mace**: MACE machine learning potentials [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L63-L66)
- **orb**: ORB machine learning potentials [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L68-L72)

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L16-L34), [pyproject.toml](/pyproject.toml#L1-L72)

## Your First Simulation

The minimal workflow for running a DIMOS simulation consists of four steps: loading a force field, selecting an integrator, initializing the simulation, and running dynamics. This pattern applies across both classical force fields and machine learning potentials.

### Basic Workflow Example

Here's a complete example running an alanine dipeptide simulation with an Amber force field:

```python
import dimos
import parmed
import torch

# Step 1: Load the force field from Amber topology file
system = dimos.AmberForceField("config.prmtop", 
                               cutoff=10, 
                               nonbonded_type="PME",
                               periodic=True)

# Step 2: Initialize positions from coordinate file
rst7_file = parmed.amber.Rst7("config.rst7")
positions = torch.tensor(rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.angstrom))

# Step 3: Create an integrator (Langevin thermostat)
dt = 0.5  # timestep in femtoseconds
T = 300   # temperature in Kelvin
gamma = 1.0  # friction coefficient
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(dt, T, gamma, system)

# Step 4: Set up the simulation
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(system, integrator, positions, temperature=T)

# Step 5: Run dynamics
num_steps = 1000
simulation.step(num_steps)
```

### Architecture Overview

DIMOS follows a modular architecture where each component handles a specific aspect of molecular simulation:

```mermaid
graph TB
    subgraph "Force Field Layer"
        FF["AmberForceField/GromacsForceField"]
        Param["Parameters from topology"]
        Energy["Energy Calculator"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Integration Layer"
        Integrator["LangevinDynamics/VelocityVerlet"]
        Accel["Update positions & velocities"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Simulation Layer"
        Sim["MDSimulation"]
        State["Manage state: pos, vel, box"]
        Neighbor["Neighbor list handling"]
    end
    
    subgraph "Optional: ML Layer"
        ML["MACE/ORB Potentials"]
        Hybrid["Hybrid ML/MM"]
    end
    
    FF --> Energy
    Integrator --> Accel
    Energy --> Sim
    Accel --> Sim
    Sim --> State
    Sim --> Neighbor
    ML --> Hybrid
    Hybrid --> Energy
    
    style FF fill:#e1f5fe
    style Integrator fill:#fff3e0
    style Sim fill:#f3e5f5
    style ML fill:#e8f5e9
```

The architecture separates concerns: force fields compute energies and forces, integrators propagate equations of motion, and simulation objects orchestrate the workflow while managing system state and periodic boundary conditions.

Sources: [README.md](/README.md#L36-L44), [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L375-L386), [dimos/integrators.py](/dimos/integrators.py#L375-L381), [dimos/simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L375-L394)

## Component Selection Guide

DIMOS provides multiple options for each simulation component. Understanding when to use each helps you build efficient simulations appropriate for your scientific questions.

### Force Field Options

| Force Field | Input Format | Best For | Nonbonded Methods |
|-------------|--------------|----------|-------------------|
| AmberForceField | `.prmtop`, `.inpcrd` | Biomolecules, standard MD | Cutoff, PME, Ewald |
| GromacsForceField | `.top`, `.gro` | Large systems, custom FFs | Cutoff, PME |

The force field classes inherit from `ClassicalParmedForceField`, which handles parameter parsing and energy calculations [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L571-L572). Both support key nonbonded treatment methods:

- **Cutoff**: Simple truncation with optional switching function
- **PME**: Particle Mesh Ewald for long-range electrostatics
- **Ewald**: Traditional Ewald summation

Sources: [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L1367-L1387), [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](/benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L45-L47)

### Integrator Selection

| Integrator | Use Case | Parameters | Key Features |
|------------|----------|------------|--------------|
| LangevinDynamics | NVT ensemble, sampling | timestep, temperature, friction | Stochastic thermostat, robust |
| VelocityVerlet | Energy conservation studies | timestep | Deterministic, NVE ensemble |
| NoseHooverChainDynamics | Precise temperature control | timestep, temperature, chain_length | Extended system, minimal perturbation |

The `CommonIntegrator` base class provides a unified interface for all integrators [dimos/integrators.py](/dimos/integrators.py#L392-L393). Integrators update particle positions and velocities based on forces computed by the force field.

Sources: [dimos/integrators.py](/dimos/integrators.py#L392-L393), [tests/test_nve.py](/tests/test_nve.py#L405-L406)

### Running Simulation Steps

Once initialized, use the `step()` method to advance the simulation:

```python
# Run a single step
simulation.step(1)

# Run multiple steps with periodic output
for i in range(100):
    simulation.step(10)
    energy = simulation.measure_potential_energy()
    print(f"Step {i*10}: PE = {energy:.2f}")
```

The simulation automatically handles neighbor list updates, boundary conditions, and energy calculations. For memory efficiency in long simulations, use `detach_()` to break the computational graph while keeping positions differentiable [dimos/simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L668-L676).

> [!TIP]
> The `detach_()` method is crucial for ML training workflows: it clears accumulated gradients from integrator state while preserving differentiability of positions for energy-based loss calculations. Call it periodically during optimization loops to prevent GPU memory overflow.

Sources: [dimos/simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L620-L636), [dimos/simulation.py](/dimos/simulation.py#L668-L676)

The repository includes ready-to-run examples demonstrating common use cases. These scripts serve as templates for your own simulations and cover both classical and ML-enhanced workflows.

### Running the Water Benchmark

A simple test simulation is available in [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](/benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L1-L80). This script simulates a water box with configurable parameters:

```bash
cd benchmark/water
python dimos_water.py dimosCPU PME 20 64 64
```

Parameters:
- Tool: `dimosCPU`, `dimosCUDA`, or `OpenMMCPU`
- Nonbonded: `Cutoff`, `PME`, or `Ewald`
- Box size: 20-140 (number of water molecules)
- Force field precision: 32 or 64
- Integration precision: 32 or 64

Sources: [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](/benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L25-L47), [examples/README.md](/examples/README.md#L1)

## Key Configuration Parameters

When setting up simulations, careful parameter selection determines accuracy and performance. These are the most commonly adjusted settings.

### Time Integration Parameters

| Parameter | Default | Range | Guidelines |
|-----------|---------|-------|------------|
| timestep | 0.5 fs | 0.1-2.0 fs | Smaller for stability, larger for speed |
| friction (Langevin) | 1.0 ps⁻¹ | 0.1-10.0 ps⁻¹ | Higher = stronger thermostat coupling |
| cutoff | 9-10 Å | 8-12 Å | Match force field recommendations |
| switch_distance | 7.5 Å | 0.75×cutoff | Smoothing function start point |

> [!TIP]
> For biomolecular simulations with Amber force fields, use `timestep=0.5 fs` with constraints on bonds involving hydrogen. This maintains energy conservation while enabling efficient sampling. Larger timesteps require constraint algorithms (handled automatically by Amber force fields).

Sources: [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](/benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L19-L21), [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L625-L638)

## Machine Learning Integration (Preview)

DIMOS uniquely supports hybrid classical/ML simulations, where part of the system uses machine learning potentials (MACE, ORB) while the remainder uses classical force fields. This enables accurate simulations of reactive regions within larger biomolecular contexts.

### Converting to ML Potentials

```python
# Start with classical system
system = dimos.AmberForceField("protein.prmtop", "protein.rst7")

# Convert a subset to MACE
mace_system = system.as_mace_system("small", atom_range=slice(100, 150))

# The system now uses ML for specified atoms, classical for rest
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(mace_system, integrator, positions)
```

The `as_mace_system()` and `as_orb_system()` methods seamlessly integrate ML potentials while preserving the same simulation interface [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L1268-L1276), [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L1322-L1328).

Sources: [dimos/ff.py](/dimos/ff.py#L1268-L1328), [experiments/dimos_hmc.py](/experiments/dimos_hmc.py#L58-L73)

# Installation and Setup



This guide provides comprehensive instructions for installing and configuring DIMOS (Differentiable Molecular Simulator), a PyTorch-based framework for molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations. Installation is designed to be straightforward while offering flexibility for different use cases, from basic simulations to advanced machine learning workflows.

## System Requirements and Prerequisites

Before installing DIMOS, ensure your system meets the minimum requirements. The framework is built on modern Python and PyTorch technology, requiring Python 3.10 or higher. The core dependencies are intentionally minimal: PyTorch (≥2.4.1) provides the computational backend and automatic differentiation, ParmEd (≥4.2.2) handles molecular topology files, and NumPy (<2.0.0) supports numerical operations. The modular design allows you to install additional components only when needed for your specific simulation requirements, such as machine learning potentials or advanced sampling methods.

![DIMOS Logo](https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS/blob/public-branch/dimos-logo.svg?raw=true)

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L25-L31), [README.md](README.md#L1-L10)

## Installation Methods

### Basic Installation via pip

The quickest way to get started with DIMOS is through pip, which installs the core package with all essential dependencies. This method is ideal for users who want to immediately begin running standard molecular dynamics simulations without needing machine learning potentials or development tools. Simply execute `pip install dimos-torch` from your command line to install the latest stable version. This approach provides a clean installation that includes the core force field systems, integrators, and simulation orchestration components required for most standard workflows.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L26-L31)

### Development Installation from Source

For users who need access to the latest features, want to modify the code, or require optional dependencies, installing from source is the recommended approach. Clone the repository and install in editable mode with specific dependency groups tailored to your needs. The editable installation (`-e` flag) allows you to modify the source code and have changes immediately reflected without reinstallation. You can selectively install dependency groups: `dev` for development tools including OpenMM and documentation building, `mmtools` for enhanced molecular mechanics capabilities, `mace` for MACE machine learning potentials, and `orb` for ORB model support.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L33-L39), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L33-L58)

```bash
git clone https://github.com/nec-research/dimos.git
cd dimos
python -m pip install -e '.[dev,mmtools,mace,orb]'
```

The following flowchart illustrates the installation decision process and available options:

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Start Installation] --> B{Installation Type}
    B -->|Quick Start| C["pip install dimos-torch"]
    B -->|Development/Custom| D[Clone Repository]
    D --> E["cd dimos"]
    E --> F{Select Dependencies}
    F --> G[Core Only]
    F --> H["dev: OpenMM, Sphinx"]
    F --> I["mmtools: Enhanced MM"]
    F --> J["mace: ML Potentials"]
    F --> K["orb: ML Potentials"]
    F --> L[All Optional]
    G --> M["pip install -e ."]
    H --> N["pip install -e '.[dev]'"]
    I --> N
    J --> N
    K --> N
    L --> N
    M --> O[Installation Complete]
    N --> O
    C --> O
```

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L26-L39), [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L1-L61)

## Dependency Groups and Optional Components

DIMOS uses a modular dependency system that allows you to install only the components you need. This approach keeps your environment clean and reduces potential conflicts while providing flexibility for advanced use cases. Understanding these groups helps you make informed decisions about which components to install based on your simulation requirements.

The following table provides a detailed breakdown of each dependency group, its purpose, and when to use it:

| Dependency Group | Purpose | Key Packages | Use Case |
|----------------|---------|-------------|----------|
| Core (default) | Basic MD/MC simulations | torch, ParmEd, numpy | Standard simulations, energy calculations |
| dev | Development and testing | openmm[cuda12], sphinx, matplotlib | Contributing to DIMOS, running test suite, building documentation |
| mmtools | Enhanced molecular mechanics | openmmtools, mdtraj, pymbar, numba | Advanced sampling, free energy calculations, enhanced validation |
| mace | MACE machine learning potentials | mace-torch≤0.3.11, cuequivariance-ops | ML-accelerated simulations, hybrid ML/MM systems |
| orb | ORB machine learning potentials | orb-models, pynanoflann | Alternative ML potentials, differentiable training workflows |

Sources: [pyproject.toml](pyproject.toml#L33-L58)

### Optional: TorchMD Dependencies

For users who want to run test cases based on torchMD for benchmarking or comparative studies, additional packages are required. To avoid installing the proprietary moleculekit dependency, install torchMD components with the `--no-deps` flag: `pip install torchmd scipy networkx pandas tqdm pyyaml --no-deps`. This allows you to perform performance comparisons between DIMOS and torchMD frameworks as demonstrated in the benchmark scripts.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L41-L44)

## Verification and Installation Testing

After installation, verify your setup by running the test suite to ensure all components are correctly installed and functioning. The repository includes comprehensive tests that validate energy correctness, simulation stability, and integration with different force field formats. Start with basic tests like `test_energy_correctness.py` which validates all energy components including various electrostatic interaction treatments. For GPU setups, tests like `test_nve.py` verify energy conservation in microcanonical ensembles, comparing DIMOS results against OpenMM reference implementations for numerical accuracy validation.

The `examples/` directory contains production-ready input files for reproducing results from published research, including both Amber and Gromacs format files. These examples serve as excellent starting points for understanding how to prepare your own simulation systems and validate your installation against known reference data.

Sources: [tests/README.md](tests/README.md#L1-L3), [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L1-L1), [tests/test_nve.py](tests/test_nve.py#L374-L419)

## Project Structure and Organization

Understanding the DIMOS project structure helps you navigate the codebase and find relevant components for your simulations. The repository is organized into logical directories separating core functionality, examples, benchmarks, tests, and experiments. This modular architecture supports both easy exploration and maintainability as the framework evolves.

![Project Structure Visualization](https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS/tree/public-branch)

The main `dimos/` directory contains all core simulation components organized by functionality: force field systems (`ff.py`), integrators (`integrators.py`), energy calculations (`energy.py`), simulation orchestration (`simulation.py`), and specialized modules for advanced methods, machine learning integration (`mlip/`), and hybrid ML/MM systems (`mlmm.py`). The `benchmark/` directory provides performance testing scripts for both water and protein systems, demonstrating how to set up and run comparative benchmarks. The `examples/` directory contains Amber and Gromacs input files for various molecular systems, serving as templates for your own simulations.

Sources: [dimos/__init__.py](dimos/__init__.py#L374-L389), [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L1-L22), [benchmark/proteins/benchmark_proteins.py](benchmark/proteins/benchmark_proteins.py#L1-L18)

## Quick Start Verification

After completing installation, verify your setup with a simple simulation to ensure everything works correctly. The following minimal example demonstrates the complete workflow from system initialization to simulation execution:

```python
import dimos
import parmed

# Load Amber force field and initialize positions
system = dimos.AmberForceField("config.prmtop", cutoff=10, nonbonded_type="PME")
rst7 = parmed.amber.Rst7("config.rst7")
positions = rst7.positions

# Set up integrator and simulation
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(dt=0.5, T=300, gamma=1.0, system=system)
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(system, integrator, positions, temperature=300)

# Run simulation
simulation.step(1000)  # 1000 steps
```

This example demonstrates the three core components of any DIMOS simulation: force field setup (system), dynamics choice (integrator), and simulation orchestration (MDSimulation). You can explore different force field formats (`GromacsForceField`), integrators (`VelocityVerlet`, `NoseHooverDynamics`), and simulation parameters to match your specific requirements.

> [!TIP]
> When installing with GPU support, ensure your CUDA driver version matches the PyTorch CUDA version. Use `torch.cuda.is_available()` to verify GPU recognition after installation.

Sources: [README.md](README.md#L46-L54), [dimos/__init__.py](dimos/__init__.py#L374-L389)

# Basic MD Simulation Workflow



This guide introduces the fundamental workflow for running molecular dynamics simulations with DIMOS, designed specifically for developers getting started with the framework. You'll learn the essential components needed to set up and execute a basic MD simulation, from system initialization to running dynamics and analyzing results.

## Understanding the Simulation Architecture

Before diving into code, it's important to understand how DIMOS organizes molecular dynamics simulations through three core components that work together:

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    subgraph Setup["Phase 1: System Setup"]
        A[Force Field] --> B[Integrator]
        B --> C[Simulation]
    end
    
    subgraph Execution["Phase 2: Simulation Execution"]
        C --> D[Energy Minimization]
        D --> E[MD Stepping]
    end
    
    subgraph Output["Phase 3: Analysis"]
        E --> F[Energy Measurements]
        E --> G[Trajectory Output]
    end
    
    A -->|provides energy function| C
    B -->|defines time propagation| C
```

The **Force Field** defines your molecular system's physics by reading topology files and computing energies. The **Integrator** determines how atoms move through time using algorithms like Velocity Verlet or Langevin dynamics. The **Simulation** orchestrates everything, managing state, applying constraints, and running the simulation loop. This separation enables flexible mixing and matching of different components while keeping the workflow simple.

## Step-by-Step Workflow

### Step 1: Set Up Your Force Field System

The first step is to create a force field system by loading your molecular topology. DIMOS supports both AMBER and GROMACS format files through specialized classes:

```python
import dimos
import torch

# For AMBER format files
system = dimos.AmberForceField(
    "config.prmtop",           # Topology file
    cutoff=10.0,               # Nonbonded cutoff in Angstroms
    switch_distance=7.5,       # Switching function distance
    nonbonded_type="Cutoff",   # Can be "Cutoff", "PME", or "Ewald"
    periodic=True              # Enable periodic boundary conditions
)

# For GROMACS format files
system = dimos.GromacsForceField(
    "system.top",              # Topology file
    "system.gro",              # Coordinate file
    cutoff=10.0,
    switch_distance=7.5,
    nonbonded_type="PME",
    periodic=True
)
```

The force field initialization loads all bonded and nonbonded parameters from your topology file, constructs energy calculation components, and sets up the simulation box dimensions based on your coordinate file.

Sources: [dimos/ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L625-L698), [dimos/ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L1367-L1378)

### Step 2: Choose and Configure Your Integrator

The integrator determines how positions and velocities are updated at each timestep. For basic simulations, you'll typically choose between:

```python
# Velocity Verlet - constant energy (NVE) ensemble
integrator = dimos.VelocityVerlet(
    timestep=0.5,              # Timestep in femtoseconds
    sys=system                 # Your force field system
)

# Langevin Dynamics - constant temperature (NVT) ensemble
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(
    timestep=0.5,              # Timestep in femtoseconds
    temperature=300.0,         # Target temperature in Kelvin
    friction=1.0,              # Friction coefficient in 1/ps
    sys=system
)

# Nose-Hoover - advanced thermostat for NVT
integrator = dimos.NoseHooverDynamics(
    timestep=2.0,              # Can use larger timestep with constraints
    temperature=300.0,
    collision_frequency=0.05,
    sys=system
)
```

Sources: [dimos/integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L836-L904), [dimos/integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L1084-L1194), [dimos/integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L1653-L1754)

### Step 3: Load Initial Coordinates

Load your initial atomic positions from coordinate files:

```python
import parmed

# From AMBER restart files
rst7_file = parmed.amber.Rst7("system.rst7")
positions = torch.tensor(
    rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.angstrom)
)

# Or use DIMOS helper for GROMACS files
positions = dimos.read_positions("system.gro")
```

Positions should be provided as PyTorch tensors with shape `(num_atoms, 3)` in Angstroms. DIMOS automatically converts these to internal units for computation.

Sources: [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L34-L37), [tests/test_nve.py](tests/test_nve.py#L391-L395)

### Step 4: Create the Simulation Object

Now combine your system, integrator, and positions into a simulation object:

```python
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(
    sys=system,                # Force field system
    integrator=integrator,     # Integrator instance
    initial_pos=positions,     # Initial positions tensor
    initial_vel=None,          # Optional: provide velocities
    temperature=300.0,         # Required if initial_vel is None
    seed=42,                   # Random seed for reproducibility
    neighbor_check_interval=1  # Neighbor list update frequency
)
```

If you don't provide initial velocities, DIMOS automatically samples them from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at the specified temperature. The simulation object also initializes neighbor lists for efficient nonbonded calculations and applies any bond constraints defined in your force field.

Sources: [dimos/simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L572-L620)

### Step 5: Energy Minimization (Recommended)

Before starting dynamics, it's good practice to minimize energy to remove any steric clashes or high-energy configurations:

```python
# Minimize using LBFGS (recommended for accuracy)
simulation.minimize_energy(
    num_optim=500,             # Number of optimization steps
    print_details=True,        # Print progress
    optimizer="LBFGS"
)

# Or use Adam for faster (but less thorough) minimization
simulation.minimize_energy(
    num_optim=100,
    optimizer="Adam"
)
```

Energy minimization uses PyTorch's optimizers to find a local energy minimum by gradient descent. LBFGS is generally preferred for its accuracy, while Adam can be faster for very large systems.

Sources: [dimos/simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L448-L510)

### Step 6: Run the Simulation

Execute dynamics using the `step()` method:

```python
# Run 10,000 steps
simulation.step(num_steps=10000)

# Or run in blocks for periodic measurements/output
for block in range(100):
    simulation.step(num_steps=100)
    
    # Measure potential energy
    pe = simulation.measure_potential_energy()
    print(f"Block {block}: PE = {pe.item()}")
```

The `step()` method advances the simulation by integrating equations of motion, applying periodic boundary conditions, updating neighbor lists, and optionally detaching from the computation graph to save memory.

Sources: [dimos/simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L620-L680)

### Step 7: (Optional) Save Trajectory

Save atomic positions for visualization or analysis:

```python
# Write PDB file with current configuration
system.write_pdb(
    positions=simulation.pos,
    output="output.pdb",
    unwrap=True                # Unwrap molecules across periodic boundaries
)
```

This writes the current configuration in PDB format, which can be visualized with tools like VMD or PyMOL.

Sources: [dimos/ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L1224-L1268)

## Complete Example: Basic NVE Simulation

Here's a complete working example combining all steps:

```python
import dimos
import torch
import parmed

# 1. Set up the force field system
system = dimos.AmberForceField(
    "examples/amber/ala2_solv.prmtop",
    cutoff=9.0,
    switch_distance=7.5,
    nonbonded_type="Cutoff",
    periodic=True
)

# 2. Create integrator (NVE ensemble)
integrator = dimos.VelocityVerlet(timestep=0.5, sys=system)

# 3. Load initial coordinates
rst7_file = parmed.amber.Rst7("examples/amber/ala2_solv.rst7")
positions = torch.tensor(rst7_file.positions.value_in_unit(parmed.unit.angstrom))

# 4. Create simulation object
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(
    system, integrator, positions, 
    temperature=600.0           # Initial high temperature
)

# 5. Minimize energy
print("Minimizing energy...")
simulation.minimize_energy(500, print_details=False)

# 6. Run production simulation
print("Running MD simulation...")
for step in range(100):
    simulation.step(num_steps=10)
    
    # Measure energies
    pe = simulation.measure_potential_energy()
    ke = simulation.measure_kinetic_energy()
    print(f"Step {step*10}: PE = {pe.item():.2f}, KE = {ke.item():.2f}")

# 7. Save final configuration
system.write_pdb(simulation.pos, "final_config.pdb")
```

Sources: [tests/test_nve.py](tests/test_nve.py#L384-L430)

## Configuration Parameters Reference

| Component | Parameter | Description | Typical Values |
|-----------|-----------|-------------|----------------|
| **Force Field** | `cutoff` | Nonbonded cutoff distance | 9.0-12.0 Å |
| | `switch_distance` | Distance where switching function starts | 7.5-9.0 Å |
| | `nonbonded_type` | Long-range electrostatics method | "Cutoff", "PME", "Ewald" |
| **Integrator** | `timestep` | Integration step size | 0.5 fs (no constraints), 2.0 fs (with constraints) |
| | `temperature` | Target temperature | 300 K (room temp) |
| | `friction` | Langevin friction coefficient | 1.0-5.0 ps⁻¹ |
| **Simulation** | `neighbor_check_interval` | Frequency to rebuild neighbor lists | 1-10 steps |
| | `seed` | Random number generator seed | Any integer |

## Common Ensemble Choices

Different ensembles are suitable for different simulation goals:

| Ensemble | Integrator | When to Use | Key Features |
|----------|------------|-------------|--------------|
| **NVE** | VelocityVerlet | Testing energy conservation, pure dynamics | Constant energy, no thermostat |
| **NVT** | LangevinDynamics | Simulations at constant temperature | Stochastic thermostat, flexible |
| **NVT** | NoseHooverDynamics | High-precision temperature control | Deterministic thermostat, good for sampling |

> [!TIP]
> For production simulations with constraints (like SHAKE on bonds involving hydrogen), you can use larger timesteps (2.0 fs) with the LangevinDynamics or NoseHooverDynamics integrators. Remember to set `constraint_option="h_angles"` when creating your force field to enable hydrogen bond angle constraints.

## Memory Optimization and Performance

DIMOS provides several options to optimize memory usage during long simulations:

```python
# Detach from computation graph (default behavior saves memory)
simulation.step(num_steps=100, detach=True)

# Keep computation graph for backpropagation (uses more memory)
simulation.step(num_steps=100, detach=False)

# Optional: use torch.compile for significant speedup
from torch import compile
compiled_step = compile(simulation.step, mode="max-autotune")
compiled_step(num_steps=100)
```

The `detach` parameter controls whether the computation graph is preserved. For standard production simulations where you don't need gradients, `detach=True` (the default) dramatically reduces memory usage by preventing PyTorch from tracking intermediate tensors.

Sources: [dimos/simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L668-L676), [benchmark/water/dimos_water.py](benchmark/water/dimos_water.py#L54-L58)

## Troubleshooting Common Issues

| Issue | Likely Cause | Solution |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| **NaN in positions** | Forces too large, timestep too big | Reduce timestep, minimize energy first |
| **Energy drift** | Integrator not appropriate | Use proper thermostat for NVT, check cutoff |
| **Slow performance** | Small neighbor check interval | Increase `neighbor_check_interval` |
| **Constraint violations** | Timestep too large for constrained bonds | Reduce timestep or disable constraints |

## Next Steps

Now that you understand the basic MD simulation workflow, you can explore more advanced topics:

- Learn about **different integrator algorithms** in [Velocity Verlet Integration](11-velocity-verlet-integration)
- Understand **temperature control methods** in [Langevin Dynamics and Thermostats](12-langevin-dynamics-and-thermostats)
- Explore **force field architecture** in [Force Field Systems Architecture](6-force-field-systems-architecture)
- See **practical examples** in [Running Your First Simulation](5-running-your-first-simulation)

# Running Your First Simulation



This guide walks you through running your first molecular dynamics simulation with DIMOS. You'll learn the core workflow, set up a simple system, and execute simulations with different integrators and options. By the end, you'll be equipped to simulate protein systems, water boxes, or custom molecular systems with confidence.

![DIMOS Logo](https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS/blob/public-branch/dimos-logo.svg?raw=true)

## Understanding DIMOS Simulation Architecture

Before diving into code, let's understand how DIMOS organizes simulations. The framework follows a modular design where each component has a specific responsibility, making it easy to customize and extend.

```mermaid
flowchart TD
    A[Force Field Setup] --> B[Integrator Selection]
    B --> C[Simulation Initialization]
    C --> D[Energy Minimization]
    D --> E[Production Run]
    E --> F[Analysis & Output]
    
    A --> A1[AmberForceField<br/>GromacsForceField]
    B --> B1[LangevinDynamics<br/>VelocityVerlet<br/>NoseHooverDynamics]
    C --> C1[MDSimulation<br/>MCSimulation]
    D --> D1[L-BFGS / SGD / Adam]
    E --> E1[step num_steps<br/>measure energies]
    F --> F1[PDB trajectories<br/>Energy logs]
```

The simulation architecture consists of three core layers working together:

1. **System Layer** (`dimos.ff`) - Defines molecular topology, force field parameters, and energy calculations. The `AmberForceField` and `GromacsForceField` classes handle loading topology files and setting up nonbonded interaction schemes.

2. **Integrator Layer** (`dimos.integrators`) - Governs how the system evolves through time. Options range from simple velocity Verlet to sophisticated thermostats like Langevin dynamics and Nose-Hoover chains.

3. **Simulation Layer** (`dimos.simulation`) - Orchestrates the entire process, managing state (positions, velocities), performing steps, and handling boundary conditions and constraints.

This modular design means you can mix and match components: use any integrator with any force field, switch between molecular dynamics and Monte Carlo simulations, or add machine learning potentials to classical systems.

Sources: [simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L403-L512), [ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L571-L639), [integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L392-L566)

## Prerequisites and Setup

To run your first simulation, you'll need simulation files containing molecular topology and initial coordinates. DIMOS provides example files in the `examples/` directory, or you can use your own Amber/Gromacs files.

### Available Example Systems

| System | Location | Type | Description |
|--------|----------|------|-------------|
| Alanine dipeptide (solvated) | `examples/amber/ala2_solv.*` | Amber | Small peptide in water, good for testing |
| Alanine pentapeptide | `examples/amber/ala5_gas.*` | Amber | Larger peptide, gas phase |
| 6N4O protein | `examples/amber/6n4o.*` | Amber | Medium-sized protein system |
| Alanine dipeptide (no constraints) | `examples/gromacs/ala2_no_constraint.*` | Gromacs | Simple test system |
| DHFR protein | `examples/gromacs/dhfr_pme.*` | Gromacs | Larger protein with PME setup |

![Project Structure](https://github.com/nec-research/DIMOS/blob/public-branch/.github/project-structure.png)

Ensure you have these files available or have prepared your own system using standard tools like `tleap` (for Amber) or `gmx pdb2gmx` (for Gromacs).

Sources: [examples/README.md](examples/README.md#L1)

## Quick Start: Your First Simulation in 5 Steps

Let's run a basic molecular dynamics simulation of alanine dipeptide in water. This example uses Langevin dynamics for temperature control, which is robust and widely applicable.

```mermaid
flowchart LR
    Step1[1. Import DIMOS<br/>Load files] --> Step2[2. Create Force Field<br/>System]
    Step2 --> Step3[3. Setup Integrator<br/>with parameters]
    Step3 --> Step4[4. Initialize<br/>Simulation]
    Step4 --> Step5[5. Run simulation<br/>& measure]
```

### Step 1: Import DIMOS and Load Input Files

```python
import dimos
import torch

# Set precision and device (optional but recommended)
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)

# Define file paths
prmtop_filename = "./examples/amber/ala2_solv.prmtop"
rst7_filename = "./examples/amber/ala2_solv.rst7"

# Load initial positions using DIMOS utility
positions = dimos.read_positions(rst7_filename)
```

The `read_positions()` function handles file parsing and unit conversion automatically, returning positions as a PyTorch tensor in the correct units (Angstroms for Amber systems by default).

Sources: [utils.py](dimos/utils.py#L667-L700)

### Step 2: Create the Force Field System

```python
# Create force field system with PME for electrostatics
system = dimos.AmberForceField(
    prmtop_filename,
    nonbonded_type="PME",           # Particle Mesh Ewald for accurate electrostatics
    cutoff=10.0,                     # Nonbonded cutoff in Angstroms
    switch_distance=7.5,             # Switching function distance
    dispersion_correction=True,      # Apply long-range dispersion correction
    periodic=True                    # Enable periodic boundary conditions
)
```

The `AmberForceField` class reads the parameter file and sets up all bonded and nonbonded interactions. Key parameters:

- **nonbonded_type**: Controls electrostatic treatment ("Cutoff", "Ewald", "PME", or None)
- **cutoff**: Distance at which nonbonded interactions are truncated
- **switch_distance**: Where the switching function begins to smoothly zero interactions
- **dispersion_correction**: Compensates for truncated Lennard-Jones interactions
- **periodic**: Whether to apply periodic boundary conditions

Sources: [ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L625-L670)

### Step 3: Configure the Integrator

```python
# Set simulation parameters
timestep = 0.5        # femtoseconds
temperature = 300.0   # Kelvin
friction = 1.0        # friction coefficient (ps^-1) for Langevin dynamics

# Create Langevin dynamics integrator
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(
    timestep,
    temperature,
    friction,
    system
)
```

Langevin dynamics combines deterministic forces with stochastic thermal noise and friction, providing automatic temperature control. The friction parameter (in ps⁻¹) controls how strongly the system couples to the thermal bath—typical values range from 0.1 to 10.0 ps⁻¹.

Sources: [integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L1084-L1140)

### Step 4: Initialize the Simulation

```python
# Create MD simulation object
simulation = dimos.simulation.MDSimulation(
    system,
    integrator,
    positions,
    temperature=temperature,    # For Maxwell-Boltzmann velocity initialization
    seed=42                     # Random seed for reproducibility
)
```

The `MDSimulation` constructor handles several critical tasks:

1. **Velocity Initialization**: If velocities aren't provided, it generates them from a Maxwell-Boltzmann distribution at the specified temperature
2. **Constraint Application**: Applies any bond/angle constraints defined in the force field
3. **Neighbor List Setup**: Initializes neighbor lists for efficient nonbonded calculations
4. **Acceleration Calculation**: Computes initial forces and accelerations

Sources: [simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L572-L620)

### Step 5: Run and Measure

```python
# Minimize energy (optional but recommended)
print("Minimizing energy...")
simulation.minimize_energy(num_optim=20, print_details=True)

# Run production simulation
num_steps = 1000
measure_every = 100

print(f"Running {num_steps} steps...")
for step in range(0, num_steps, measure_every):
    simulation.step(measure_every)
    
    # Measure properties
    pe = simulation.measure_potential_energy()
    ke = simulation.measure_kinetic_energy()
    temp = simulation.sys.measure_temperature(simulation.vel)
    
    print(f"Step {step}: PE={pe:.2f}, KE={ke:.2f}, Total={pe+ke:.2f}, T={temp:.1f}K")

print("Simulation complete!")
```

> [!TIP]
> Always minimize energy before production runs—this removes bad contacts and prevents numerical instability during the first few steps.

The `step()` method advances the simulation by the specified number of steps, updating positions and velocities according to the integrator's algorithm. It automatically handles periodic boundary conditions, neighbor list updates, and constraint enforcement.

Sources: [simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L620-L680)

## Alternative Simulation Workflows

### Gromacs Systems

For Gromacs users, the workflow is nearly identical:

```python
import dimos
import torch

# Load Gromacs files
system = dimos.GromacsForceField(
    "system.top", 
    "system.gro",
    nonbonded_type="PME",
    cutoff=10.0,
    switch_distance=7.5,
    periodic=True
)

positions = dimos.read_positions("system.gro")

# Rest of simulation setup identical to Amber example
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(0.5, 300.0, 1.0, system)
simulation = dimos.MDSimulation(system, integrator, positions, temperature=300.0)
```

Sources: [ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L1434-L1450), [utils.py](dimos/utils.py#L667-L700)

### Velocity Verlet (NVE Ensemble)

For energy conservation studies, use Velocity Verlet without a thermostat:

```python
integrator = dimos.VelocityVerlet(timestep, system)
simulation = dimos.simulation.MDSimulation(
    system,
    integrator,
    positions,
    temperature=300.0  # Only used for initial velocity distribution
)

# In NVE, temperature will drift according to energy exchange
simulation.step(1000)
```

Sources: [integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L836-L907)

### Nose-Hoover Thermostat

For more sophisticated temperature control:

```python
integrator = dimos.NoseHooverDynamics(
    timestep=2.0,
    temperature=300.0,
    collision_frequency=0.05,
    sys=system
)
```

Sources: [integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L1653-L1813)

## Writing Trajectory Files

To save configurations during simulation:

```python
output_file = open("trajectory.pdb", "w")

for step in range(0, num_steps, 100):
    simulation.step(100)
    
    # Write current configuration to PDB
    system.write_pdb(simulation.pos, output_file)
    output_file.flush()

output_file.close()
```

The `write_pdb()` method handles unit conversion and formatting automatically. For periodic systems, it can optionally unwrap coordinates.

Sources: [ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L1224-L1268)

## Complete Working Example

Here's a complete script combining all elements:

```python
import dimos
import torch

# Setup
torch.set_default_dtype(torch.float64)
torch.set_default_device("cpu")  # or "cuda" for GPU acceleration

# Load system
system = dimos.AmberForceField(
    "./examples/amber/ala2_solv.prmtop",
    nonbonded_type="Cutoff",
    cutoff=10.0,
    dispersion_correction=True,
    periodic=True
)

positions = dimos.read_positions("./examples/amber/ala2_solv.rst7")

# Create integrator and simulation
integrator = dimos.LangevinDynamics(0.5, 300.0, 1.0, system)
simulation = dimos.simulation.MDSimulation(
    system, 
    integrator, 
    positions, 
    temperature=300.0,
    seed=42
)

# Minimize
print("Minimizing energy...")
simulation.minimize_energy(20, print_details=True)

# Production run with output
print("Running simulation...")
output_file = open("output.pdb", "w")

num_steps = 1000
measure_interval = 100

for step in range(0, num_steps, measure_interval):
    simulation.step(measure_interval)
    
    pe = simulation.measure_potential_energy()
    ke = simulation.measure_kinetic_energy()
    temp = system.measure_temperature(simulation.vel)
    
    print(f"Step {step:5d}: E_total={pe+ke:12.2f}, T={temp:6.1f}K")
    system.write_pdb(simulation.pos, output_file)

output_file.close()
print("Done!")
```

## Common Parameters Reference

| Parameter | Typical Values | Description | Notes |
|-----------|----------------|-------------|-------|
| `timestep` | 0.5-2.0 fs | Integration step size | Larger with constraints, smaller without |
| `temperature` | 300-350 K | Target temperature | Used for velocity initialization and thermostats |
| `friction` | 0.1-10.0 ps⁻¹ | Langevin coupling strength | 1.0 ps⁻¹ is common for biomolecular simulations |
| `cutoff` | 8-12 Å | Nonbonded cutoff distance | Must be less than half box size |
| `switch_distance` | 6-10 Å | Where switching begins | Should be < cutoff |
| `nonbonded_type` | "Cutoff", "PME", "Ewald" | Electrostatic treatment | PME recommended for periodic systems |
| `constraint_option` | None, "h_angles", "all-bonds" | Constraint handling | Allows larger timesteps when used |

Sources: [ff.py](dimos/ff.py#L625-L670), [integrators.py](dimos/integrators.py#L1084-L1140)

## Troubleshooting Guide

| Issue | Likely Cause | Solution |
|-------|--------------|----------|
| NaN in positions | Bad contacts or too large timestep | Run energy minimization first, reduce timestep |
| Energy drift (NVE) | Insufficient cutoff or poor starting config | Increase cutoff, ensure proper minimization |
| Temperature not converging | Friction too low or system too small | Increase friction coefficient, check system size |
| Neighbor list errors | Cutoff too large for box | Reduce cutoff or use larger simulation box |
| Memory issues | Too many atoms or not detaching | Use `detach=True` in step(), reduce system size |

> [!TIP]
> Always check for NaN values early—if you see them in the first few steps, minimize energy before continuing.

Sources: [simulation.py](dimos/simulation.py#L668-L680)
